hook.text: E. coli doubles every 20 minutes — engineer it right and it becomes a microscopic chemical factory.

buildup.text: Metabolic engineering redirects cellular pathways — funneling carbon from growth into product synthesis.

discovery.text: Corynebacterium glutamicum produces 3 million tons of amino acids per year — feeding livestock and flavoring food.

twist.text: Host organisms fight back — cells evolve to eliminate production plasmids because making product wastes their resources.

climax.text: Adaptive laboratory evolution forces cells to optimize — running evolution in the lab to create better production strains.

punchline.text: Engineer the microbe, harvest the molecule — cell factories turn sugar into value.

quiz.question: Why do microbial cell factories lose productivity over time?
options: The production equipment wears out and needs replacement
Cells evolve to shed production genes because making product wastes resources they need for growth
The sugar feedstock degrades during fermentation

details.summary: Microbial cell factories are microorganisms engineered to efficiently produce specific chemicals, fuels, or materials. Metabolic engineering rewires cellular pathways to redirect carbon and energy toward desired products while minimizing unwanted byproducts.
details.whyItMatters: Microbial cell factories can produce sustainably what petroleum chemistry produces from fossil fuels. Engineering organisms to make chemicals from renewable feedstocks is central to building a bio-based industrial economy.
takeaways: Metabolic engineering redirects cellular metabolism toward target products
E. coli and yeast are the most commonly used chassis organisms
Titer, rate, and yield are the key performance metrics for cell factories

faq.question: Why are E. coli and yeast the most popular chassis organisms?
faq.answer: Both have well-characterized genetics, extensive genetic tool kits, fast growth rates, and decades of industrial use. E. coli excels at producing proteins and small molecules. Yeast handles larger proteins, tolerates low pH, and is food-safe for consumer products.

faq.question: What do titer, rate, and yield mean for cell factories?
faq.answer: Titer is the final product concentration in grams per liter. Rate is how fast product accumulates per hour. Yield is how much feedstock converts to product versus biomass or waste. All three must be high for commercial viability.
